title: The Python Data Model
description: How objects, references, identity, equality, and special methods form the foundation of Python's object behavior.
objectives: Understand objects, references, identity, and equality precisely
Understand mutability's role in the data model
Know the purpose of key dunder methods: __str__, __repr__, __len__, __getitem__, __iter__, __next__

content.heading: Objects, References, Identity, and Equality
content.body:
Everything in Python is an object — every int, function, class, and module. A variable is a reference (a name bound to an object), not a container holding a value directly. Object identity (checked with is, or compared numerically via id()) means 'are these two names pointing at the literal same object in memory'; equality (checked with ==, backed by a class's __eq__ method) means 'do these objects represent the same value', which is a separate, class-defined question. Two distinct objects can be equal (two separate list objects both containing [1, 2, 3]) without being identical.

Mutability determines what 'the same object, changed' looks like: mutating a list changes what every reference to that object sees, whereas 'modifying' an immutable int or str actually creates a brand-new object and rebinds the name to it.

content.heading: Special (Dunder) Methods That Define Object Behavior
content.body: The data model is largely defined by dunder methods your own classes can implement to plug into Python's built-in syntax and functions. __str__(self) backs str(obj)/print(obj) — a readable, informal representation. __repr__(self) backs repr(obj) and how an object displays inside a list/dict or at the REPL — an unambiguous, ideally-reconstructible representation; if only __repr__ is defined, Python falls back to it for str() too. __len__(self) backs len(obj) and also determines truthiness by default (an object with __len__ returning 0 is falsy). __getitem__(self, key) enables obj[key] indexing/slicing; __iter__/__next__ implement the iterator protocol (covered in the Iterators and Generators lesson). Implementing these consistently is what makes a custom class feel like a natural, 'first-class' Python type rather than a bolted-on object.

content.explanation: p1 == p2 uses the custom __eq__ to compare coordinates (True), while p1 is p2 checks object identity, which is False since they're two separately-created Point objects.

keyPoints: A variable is a reference to an object, not the object itself
is checks identity (same object); == checks equality (same value, via __eq__)
Mutability determines whether 'changing' an object affects every reference to it
Dunder methods (__str__, __repr__, __len__, __getitem__, __iter__) let custom classes participate in built-in syntax
commonMistakes: Using is to compare values, which only reliably matches for identity, not equal-but-distinct objects
Defining __eq__ without also defining __hash__, making instances unusable in sets/dicts
Confusing __str__ (informal, for humans) with __repr__ (unambiguous, for developers/debugging)
